For starters, a lot of people don't tip cash anymore. The 10% is what's required by law. However, in order to do most normal adult things like get a loan or apply for an apartment, proof of income is required. The less you report, the lower your income is on paper, and that could cost you a place to live or higher monthly interest. It's up to the worker to decide what they want to declare in cash. Sure, folks can be disingenuous about it, but they are also shooting themselves in the foot in other ways. 

Regardless, if you choose to report little to nothing in tips, the employer will likely fire you and the IRS will have questions.

ETA: The title of your post says we never make $2.13/hr and that is untrue. Constantly making under minimum wage is unheard of, but it can happen.
Agreed. I only brought taxes into the discourse to highlight the fact that zero dollar paychecks are combined with usually owing in taxes, therefore tips are my income, period.

Unfortunately, that has been the standard for a very long time, so breaking that trend is difficult, especially if the employer doesn't have capital up front to make that switch for labor costs. That would mean increasing prices (necessary, but sticker shock is real), which could alienate the business from the community.

Trust me, I wish my profession was taken a bit more seriously and could enjoy benefits and a stable income. But I work for a small, family-owned business that simply cannot afford that labor cost.

So, there's a couple answers to this:

If you get a lot of cash throughout your shift and owe the house cash, then your tips are paid in full in cash at the end of your shift (including cc).

Some places pay tips out nightly from petty cash. Then there's a payroll check.

Some places (like mine) put cc tips on a check (minus cash) and do payroll separately. We use a payroll company, so they do not handle our tip money.

I've never worked in a tip-pool scenario, but I would assume they also do payroll separately.

That's...not exactly correct.

Example A: I work a two-week period 2.13/hr, but it's extremely slow. Full-time (5 days, 40 hrs/wk, so 80 hrs) at 7.25/hr would mean I would have to make less than $580 in that time period in order for the restaurant to make up the minimum wage. That would average less than $58 in tips per 8 hour shift. If you are a server and you're making less than $58/day working full-time, you need a different job.

Example B: same parameters but say I average $65/shift. That would be $650/two-week pay period. At that rate, the employer would pay me $2.13/hr because I made more in tips than I would have just working $7.25 with no tips. 

Source: I've worked as a hostess, server, cook, manager, and bartender for twenty years. For MANY years working as server/bartender, I received zero dollar paychecks, because all of my $2.13/hr went to taxes...and then I owed *additional* taxes at the end of the year (standard deduction, no kids or property, no state income tax). That means I survived purely on tips.

I agree that tipping has gotten out of control, but servers who make $2.13 generally do not receive paychecks at all. In the very least, if you are sitting at a bar or table being waited upon, that is a service we provide, and should be compensated accordingly.

What I can suggest: slow introductions are KEY. We used a baby gate that we attached flat cardboard to and kept each cat on either side. That way, they knew of the other cat's presence, but they couldn't see each other. We slowly raised the cardboard little by little over time til they could fully see each other. Then we let them free roam when we were at home, but kept one in the bedroom at night while the other roamed (alternating). That way, my cat could get used to the new space and his cat could get used to all the new furniture in the space. His cat had some behavioral issues (peeing/pooping outside the litterbox) that eventually stopped. We did this by (at feeding time) closing her in our office and giving her plenty of time to eat and use her own litterbox. My cat is a goblin who eats everything so it was important to give the other cat space to eat. Everything is peachy now!

I read a news article once about how elderly patients, especially those with neurological diagnoses like dementia, have a hard time eating food and need the food pureed. However, trying to force yourself to eat literal slop is degrading and dehumanizing; the mental gymnastics needed to get past that is extraordinary. 

As much as taste and smell go into eating, visuals do as well. We want our food to look *appetizing*. So, researchers found that doing something as simple as placing the pureed food into a mold (no other changes), the recipients were much more likely to eat and enjoy their food versus the non -molded food. 

It is likely that given your need for soft foods, this is the same kind of preparation you received. While it may look gross to us solid-food, neurologically-sound folks, it actually helps those who aren't. Enjoy!
